label: Poisson Structures
notes: This appendix loosens the symplectic framework into the more flexible world of Poisson manifolds. We motivate why a bracket on functions, rather than a nondegenerate two-form, is the right primitive once we want to handle reduced spaces, dual Lie algebras, and rigid-body dynamics inside a single uniform language.

label: From Symplectic to Poisson
notes: Recall that every symplectic manifold already carries a Poisson bracket built from the inverse of its symplectic form. The point of this appendix is that the bracket survives even when the form degenerates, so we keep Hamiltonian mechanics while dropping the demand that the structure be invertible everywhere.

label: Axioms of the Bracket
notes: Here we lay out the four defining axioms: bilinearity, antisymmetry, the Leibniz derivation rule, and the Jacobi identity. Emphasize that Leibniz makes the bracket a first-order differential operator in each slot, while Jacobi is the deep compatibility condition that makes Hamiltonian flows close into an algebra.

label: The Poisson Bivector
notes: Leibniz forces the bracket to come from a bivector field contracting the two differentials. Walk through how the components form an antisymmetric matrix, and stress that the Jacobi identity becomes a quadratic differential equation on that bivector, the vanishing Schouten bracket, which is far from automatic.

label: Hamiltonian Vector Fields
notes: Every function defines a Hamiltonian vector field by feeding it into the bivector. Explain that the bracket of two functions equals the directional derivative of one along the other's flow, and that the map from functions to vector fields is a Lie algebra homomorphism precisely because Jacobi holds.

label: Degeneracy and Casimirs
notes: Unlike symplectic structures the bivector can drop rank. Functions whose Hamiltonian field vanishes, the Casimirs, bracket to zero with everything and form the center of the algebra. They are conserved by every Hamiltonian flow, so they label invariant subsets and behave like superselection charges of the system.

label: Symplectic Leaves
notes: The image of all Hamiltonian fields integrates into a foliation whose leaves carry a genuine symplectic form. Stress that dynamics never leaves the leaf through a starting point, that leaf dimension equals the bivector rank, and that Casimirs are exactly the functions constant along every leaf.

label: The Lie-Poisson Bracket
notes: The central example lives on the dual of a Lie algebra. The bracket evaluates the point against the commutator of the two differentials, which are themselves Lie algebra elements. This linear structure is canonical, requires no extra choices, and turns representation theory into geometry.

label: Coadjoint Orbits
notes: For the Lie-Poisson structure the symplectic leaves are precisely the coadjoint orbits of the group acting on the dual. Mention Kirillov, Kostant, and Souriau, and note that the quadratic Casimirs cut the dual into these orbits, each an even-dimensional symplectic homogeneous space.

label: Rigid Body on so(3)*
notes: Specialize to the rotation algebra, whose dual is three-dimensional angular-momentum space. The Casimir is the squared length of the momentum, so leaves are concentric spheres. Euler's rigid-body equations are exactly the Lie-Poisson flow, tracing energy-ellipsoid intersections on each fixed-radius sphere.

label: Reduction from T*G
notes: Explain that left or right translation collapses the cotangent bundle of a Lie group onto the dual of its algebra, and the canonical bracket pushes forward to the Lie-Poisson bracket. This is the abstract reason rigid bodies and ideal fluids inherit a Hamiltonian description after symmetry reduction.

label: Synthesis
notes: Close by tying the strands together: a Poisson manifold is a foliated stack of symplectic leaves indexed by Casimirs, the dual Lie algebra is the universal linear model, and reduction explains why this structure pervades mechanics. Preview that quantization and integrable systems both rest on this scaffold.
